intro: Before hunting, learn what telemetry the dataset contains and whether the fields you expect are actually there.

recipes.title: What data is loaded?
recipes.why: Every investigation starts with a data inventory. Count events per sourcetype and source to see which sensors fired.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| stats count by sourcetype source
| sort -count

recipes.title: Which Windows event IDs are present?
recipes.why: Event ID 1 is process creation, 10 is process access, 3 is network, 4688 is Security process creation. This histogram is your map of the dataset.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog
| stats count by EventCode
| sort -count

recipes.title: Are fields extracted?
recipes.why: If with_eventcode is 0, the lab field-extraction config is missing and every field-based hunt will look empty. Install it from the dashboard banner.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog
| stats count as events count(EventCode) as with_eventcode count(Image) as sysmon_processes count(NewProcessName) as security_processes

recipes.title: Read one raw event
recipes.why: SOC analysts still read raw logs. Look at the XML structure and where each field comes from.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog
| head 1
| table _time host source sourcetype _raw

intro: Turn raw events into a story: what ran, in what order, and under which parent process.

recipes.title: Process execution timeline
recipes.why: Normalize Sysmon (Image) and Security (NewProcessName) fields into one timeline. Sorting ascending shows the attacker's sequence.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog (EventCode=1 OR EventCode=4688)
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName), Account=coalesce(User, SubjectUserName)
| table _time host EventCode Process Parent CommandLine Account
| sort _time
| head 200

recipes.title: Parent → child process pairs
recipes.why: Malicious behavior usually stands out in the ancestry: cmd.exe spawning rundll32.exe, or a web server spawning PowerShell.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog (EventCode=1 OR EventCode=4688)
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName)
| stats count by Parent Process
| sort -count
| head 30

recipes.title: Rare processes (frequency analysis)
recipes.why: Rarity is a hunter's best friend. Processes that appear once or twice in a dataset deserve a look.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName)
| stats count by Process
| sort count
| head 25

recipes.title: Cross-source coverage
recipes.why: If only one sensor saw the attack, you have a visibility gap. Compare what each source recorded per host.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| stats dc(sourcetype) as source_types count as events values(sourcetype) as sourcetypes by host
| sort -events

intro: Hypothesis-driven hunts. Each query encodes a behavior, not a single indicator.

recipes.title: LSASS process access
recipes.why: Credential dumping opens lsass.exe with read/full-access rights. GrantedAccess values such as 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1438, 0x143a and 0x1fffff are strong signals.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog EventCode=10
| search TargetImage="*lsass.exe"
| eval Process=coalesce(SourceImage, Image)
| table _time host Process TargetImage GrantedAccess User
| sort -_time

recipes.title: Credential dumping command lines
recipes.why: Procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, mimikatz and pypykatz leave distinctive command lines. This is classic detection-engineering evidence.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| search CommandLine="*procdump*" OR CommandLine="*comsvcs*" OR CommandLine="*minidump*" OR CommandLine="*mimikatz*" OR Image="*mimikatz*" OR NewProcessName="*mimikatz*"
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName)
| table _time host EventCode Process Parent CommandLine
| sort -_time

recipes.title: PowerShell execution
recipes.why: Attackers love PowerShell. Look for suspicious parents, encoded arguments, and download cradle strings.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| search Image="*powershell*" OR NewProcessName="*powershell*" OR CommandLine="*powershell*"
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Account=coalesce(User, SubjectUserName)
| stats count values(CommandLine) as commands by host Account Process
| sort -count

recipes.title: Encoded or obfuscated commands
recipes.why: Base64 and encoded-command switches hide intent from casual review. Decode them before deciding.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| search CommandLine="*-enc*" OR CommandLine="*-EncodedCommand*" OR CommandLine="*FromBase64String*"
| table _time host CommandLine
| sort -_time

recipes.title: Outbound network connections
recipes.why: Sysmon Event ID 3 shows process-to-IP telemetry. Rare destinations and unusual process/port pairs are worth triage.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog EventCode=3
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName)
| stats count values(Process) as processes by DestinationIp DestinationPort Protocol
| sort -count
| head 30

recipes.title: Persistence mechanisms
recipes.why: Service installs (7045), scheduled tasks (4698/4697) and registry run keys (Sysmon 13) are common persistence paths.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog (EventCode=7045 OR EventCode=4697 OR EventCode=4698 OR EventCode=13)
| eval Detail=coalesce(ServiceName, TaskName, TargetObject)
| table _time host EventCode Detail Image CommandLine
| sort -_time
| head 100

intro: An alert is a question, not an answer. Build the timeline, decide true/false positive, and write down the evidence.

recipes.title: Attack timeline around LSASS
recipes.why: Correlate process access with the commands that caused it. This is the evidence you would attach to an incident ticket.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| search (EventCode=10 AND TargetImage="*lsass*") OR CommandLine="*lsass*"
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName)
| table _time host sourcetype EventCode Process Parent CommandLine TargetImage GrantedAccess
| sort _time
| head 200

recipes.title: Scope: which hosts and accounts?
recipes.why: Determine blast radius before escalating. Count activity per host and account.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| eval Account=coalesce(User, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName)
| stats count dc(sourcetype) as sources by host Account
| sort -count

recipes.title: Candidate detection: LSASS dumping
recipes.why: This is a small detection you can save in Splunk. It combines process access rights with known dumping command lines.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog
| search (CommandLine="*procdump*" AND CommandLine="*lsass*") OR CommandLine="*comsvcs.dll*Minidump*" OR (EventCode=10 AND TargetImage="*lsass*" AND GrantedAccess IN ("0x1010","0x1410","0x1438","0x143a","0x1fffff"))
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName)
| stats count values(CommandLine) as commands values(GrantedAccess) as access by host Process Parent
| where count > 0

recipes.title: Tune it: baseline the tool
recipes.why: Procdump is legitimate in some environments. Establish who runs it and from where before deciding it is malicious.
recipes.spl:
index=attack_data
| search CommandLine="*procdump*" OR Image="*procdump*" OR NewProcessName="*procdump*"
| eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Account=coalesce(User, SubjectUserName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName)
| stats count values(CommandLine) as commands by host Account Parent Process
| sort -count
